To assess the quality and accuracy of the summarizations within our RAPTOR model, we conducted
an analysis focusing on hallucinations in the generated summaries. The summaries were generated
by gpt-3.5-turbo and subsequently annotated to quantify the rates of hallucinations, to examine

sampling strategy provides a broad view of the model’s performance across different contexts. Each
node was annotated by hand, and determined if it contained a hallucination.

data that was not present in the text being summarized, or from incorrectly extrapolating some
information when creating the summary.

ABSTRACT
Retrieval-augmented language models can better adapt to changes in world state
and incorporate long-tail knowledge. However, most existing methods retrieve
only short contiguous chunks from a retrieval corpus, limiting holistic under-
standing of the overall document context. We introduce the novel approach of
recursively embedding, clustering, and summarizing chunks of text, constructing
a tree with differing levels of summarization from the bottom up. At inference
time, our RAPTOR model retrieves from this tree, integrating information across
lengthy documents at different levels of abstraction. Controlled experiments show
that retrieval with recursive summaries offers significant improvements over tra-
ditional retrieval-augmented LMs on several tasks. On question-answering tasks
that involve complex, multi-step reasoning, we show state-of-the-art results; for
example, by coupling RAPTOR retrieval with the use of GPT-4, we can improve
the best performance on the QuALITY benchmark by 20% in absolute accuracy.

questions.answer:
The document introduces RAPTOR (Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval), a novel method for retrieval-augmented language models. RAPTOR recursively clusters and summarizes text chunks based on their vector embeddings, constructing a tree from the bottom up. This approach allows for retrieval augmentation at different levels of abstraction, improving holistic understanding of lengthy documents [4].

The methodology involves embedding and clustering text chunks, generating summaries for each cluster, and building a hierarchical tree structure. Nodes in the tree represent clusters of text, with parent nodes containing summaries of their child nodes. This structure enables multi-scale retrieval and integration of information during inference [2].

Experiments demonstrate that RAPTOR outperforms traditional retrieval-augmented language models. When combined with GPT-4, it achieves state-of-the-art results on three question-answering (QA) tasks: NarrativeQA (free text response questions on books and movies), QASPER (full-text NLP papers), and QuALITY. For example, coupling RAPTOR with GPT-4 improves performance on the QuALITY benchmark by 20% in absolute accuracy [4].

An ablation study compares RAPTOR with a recency-based tree approach. The results show that RAPTOR achieves slightly higher accuracy (56.6%) compared to the recency-based approach (55.8%) when using SBERT embeddings and UnifiedQA [3].

The document also includes a hallucination analysis of the summaries generated by the RAPTOR model. Out of 150 nodes sampled across 40 stories, 4% (6 nodes) contained hallucinations. These hallucinations typically involved the model adding minor information from its training data or incorrectly extrapolating information not present in the original text [1].

The average compression ratio across all datasets is 72%, with an average summary length of 131 tokens and an average child node length of 86 tokens. Detailed statistics are provided for each dataset, showing variations in summary length, child node length, and compression ratios [3].

questions.answer: RAPTOR consistently outperforms both BM25 and DPR across multiple datasets and metrics. In the QuALITY dataset, RAPTOR achieves an accuracy of 62.4%, which is a 2% and 5.1% improvement over DPR and BM25, respectively [1]. When using UnifiedQA, RAPTOR outperforms DPR and BM25 by 2.7% and 6.7%, respectively [1]. In the QASPER dataset, RAPTOR achieves an F-1 score of 55.7%, which is at least 1.8% higher than DPR and at least 5.3% higher than BM25 [4]. In the NarrativeQA dataset, RAPTOR excels across multiple metrics, surpassing BM25 and DPR by margins ranging from 1.7 to 5.8 and 0.7 to 2.1 points, respectively [1]. For example, in ROUGE-L, RAPTOR surpasses BM25 and DPR by 7.3 and 2.7 points, respectively [1]. In Table 1, RAPTOR with SBERT, BM25, and DPR shows improvements in ROUGE, BLEU-1, BLEU-4, and METEOR scores compared to the same methods without RAPTOR [2]. In the QuALITY and QASPER datasets, RAPTOR with SBERT, BM25, and DPR shows improvements in accuracy and Answer F1 scores compared to the same methods without RAPTOR [5]. However, there are no explicit results that go against this trend in the provided sources. In conclusion, RAPTOR consistently outperforms BM25 and DPR across multiple datasets and metrics.

The RAPTOR system employs two retrieval strategies: **tree traversal** and **collapsed tree**, and their performance was evaluated on 20 stories from the QASPER dataset [1]. 

The **collapsed tree approach** consistently outperformed the **tree traversal method**. This is attributed to the greater flexibility of the collapsed tree, which allows for simultaneous comparison of all nodes in the tree, enabling retrieval of information at the appropriate level of granularity for a given question [1]. In contrast, the tree traversal method maintains a fixed ratio of higher-order thematic information to granular details, regardless of the question's requirements [1].

Figure 3 in the document compares the performance of these methods using different top-k values for tree traversal and varying maximum token numbers for the collapsed tree [3]. The best results were achieved with the **collapsed tree approach using 2000 tokens**, which approximately corresponds to retrieving the top-20 nodes [3]. This method ensures that the context does not exceed the model's input limitations, as token counts can vary across nodes [3].

For experiments involving the UnifiedQA model, which has a maximum context length of 512 tokens, 400 tokens of context were provided for both RAPTOR and the baseline methods [3]. 

In conclusion, the **collapsed tree method** is preferred due to its superior performance and flexibility, particularly in retrieving information that matches the required level of detail for a given query [1].
